meaning: To survive or endure to the end of a period; to hold out, keep going, or remain in supply for as long as needed — e.g. 'he won't last out the week', 'the rations must last out till spring'.
note: Reads as the phrasal verb 'to last out'. Possible it is lifted from 'first in, last out' (the accounting/queue convention, or the sense of being the last to leave), but on its own the endure/hold-out reading is the natural one.

meaning: Honours, distinctions or fame won by achievement — the laurel wreath of the victor. Chiefly used in 'rest on one's laurels' (to be so satisfied with past success that one stops striving) and 'look to one's laurels' (to guard a reputation now under threat).
note: The heading is a TRUNCATION — 'laurels' alone is a noun, not an idiom. The deck almost certainly means 'rest on one's laurels'.

meaning: To overlook someone's fault or offence; to let them off without punishment or comment on this occasion.
note: Distinguish 'let something slide' (to neglect it, allow it to deteriorate) from 'let SOMEONE slide' (to excuse them). The heading names a person, so the excuse sense.

meaning: Words chosen for the strong emotional or moral charge they carry beyond their plain meaning — language that smuggles in a judgement and prods the listener toward a conclusion (e.g. 'regime' for 'government', 'slaughter' for 'killed').

The material rewards of office or of a cause — the pay, patronage and perks people are really after when they profess high motives. From the Gospel miracle of feeding the multitude; used sardonically of those who follow a leader or a creed for what they can get out of it.
note: Usually 'the loaves and fishes', often with 'be after' or 'look to'.

meaning: To reach the top level of an activity — to become genuinely successful, famous or well paid, as opposed to scraping along in the minor ranks.
note: CORRUPT HEADING — the idiom is 'make the big time' (or 'hit the big time'); the article has been dropped.

meaning: To soften or tone down what one says, using polite, roundabout language to avoid giving offence. Almost always used in the negative — 'not to mince matters' means to speak bluntly and call things by their true names.
note: Variant of the commoner 'mince words'. In practice the deck should probably teach it as 'not to mince matters'.

idiom: Nail one’s colors to the master
meaning: To declare one's beliefs or allegiance openly and irrevocably, committing oneself with no possibility of backing down. From a ship nailing its flag to the mast so it cannot be struck in surrender.
note: CORRUPT HEADING — 'master' is a typo for 'MAST'. The whole force of the image is the mast: colours nailed there cannot be lowered, so no surrender is possible. 'Master' destroys the metaphor.

meaning: Of the very finest quality or the most pronounced degree. Originally a jeweller's grading of a diamond's clarity; now applied to excellence ('a scholar of the first water') and, ironically, to faults ('a scoundrel of the first water').
note: Worth teaching that it works for both praise and condemnation — it intensifies whatever noun it follows.

meaning: Smooth, flattering, ingratiating speech that is not sincere; the gift of saying oily, unctuous things to win favour.
By everyone, universally, on all sides — 'it is admitted on all hands that…' means every party concerned concedes it.
note: Slightly archaic/formal; the modern equivalent is 'on all sides' or 'universally'.

meaning: Out of one's senses with fear or distress — driven to the point of not being able to think straight. Nearly always after a verb of frightening: 'scared/frightened out of my wits' = terrified.
note: Heading is a FRAGMENT — the idiom needs its verb ('scared out of one's wits', 'frightened out of one's wits'). Bare 'out of my wits' is not usable on its own.

meaning: To squander recklessly, or to trifle with something and treat it as of no value — 'to play ducks and drakes with the company's money'. From the game of skimming flat stones across water, where the stone is thrown away for amusement.
note: Normally takes 'with': play ducks and drakes WITH something.

meaning: To supply a detailed plan or working model that others can follow — to lay down, in concrete terms, how something is to be done.
note: This is a COLLOCATION rather than a true idiom; 'blueprint' is the figurative element and 'provide' is ordinary. If the deck wants the idiom, it is 'a blueprint for X'.

meaning: To rescue someone from a mess at one's own risk — to do the dangerous or unpleasant work from which another gets the benefit. From the fable of the monkey using the cat's paw to rake roasting chestnuts out of the fire.
note: TRUNCATED HEADING — the idiom is 'pull someone's chestnuts out of the fire'. 'Pulled the chestnuts' loses the fire, which is where the whole point (the risk) lives.

meaning: A large family, many children. From Psalm 127 — 'Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them' — where the arrows are sons. By extension, a plentiful stock of resources or options held in reserve.
note: Two live readings and I am not sure which the deck wants. The scriptural sense (many children) is the established idiom; but modern business English uses 'another arrow in one's quiver' for an extra option or skill, and a compiler may have back-formed this heading from that.

meaning: To follow the same unvarying routine or line of thought — to go on in the old accustomed way without change or fresh ideas. Of two people, to think alike; of an institution, to be stuck in a rut.
note: Non-standard as a headword; the usual forms are 'run in a groove' or 'be in a groove'. Meaning is clear from the image (a wheel confined to one track) but I would not call this a fixed idiom.

meaning: Setting money or a resource aside for one stated purpose so that it cannot be diverted to anything else; also, walling off part of a business or a set of assets so that risk or loss elsewhere cannot reach it.
note: Chiefly financial/administrative. Common in budget and banking contexts: 'the grant is ring-fenced for teacher training'.

meaning: To reopen a painful matter that had healed over — to revive an old grievance, quarrel or humiliation that everyone had been content to leave buried.
note: NON-STANDARD FORM — should be plural, 'rip up old sores', or the commoner 'open (up) an old wound' / 'rake up old sores'. The singular without an article reads as a truncation.

meaning: To reverse or reduce something to an earlier, lower level — to undo a price rise, a regulation, a policy or an advance already made ('roll back the tax', 'roll back the frontiers of the state').
note: Note it can also mean to push an enemy or a force back the way it came.

meaning: Past tense of 'see through' — to perceive the truth behind a pretence and refuse to be taken in ('she saw through his excuses at once').
note: AMBIGUOUS HEADING, and the deck should fix it. 'Saw through' is also the literal past of sawing, and it collides with 'see something through' (to carry it on to the finish). The headword ought to be 'see through'.

meaning: To oppose something firmly and settledly; to set oneself resolutely to resist or refuse it.
note: Headword is inflected for a third-person plural subject; the dictionary form is 'set one's face against'.

meaning: To leave suddenly and without warning — to clear off, make a hurried exit, or abscond, often abandoning a duty or a person.
note: This is chiefly AUSTRALIAN/NEW ZEALAND slang ('shoot through like a Bondi tram'). A learner in an Indian exam context is unlikely to meet it, and the phrase can also be read literally (a bullet shooting through). Worth checking the deck's source.

meaning: To leave quietly and unobtrusively, without drawing attention or taking leave of anyone. Also, of clothing, to take a garment off quickly and easily.
note: Two senses (depart unnoticed / remove a garment); the first is the idiomatic one.

meaning: (1) To represent or signify — 'UN stands for United Nations'. (2) To tolerate or put up with, nearly always in the negative — 'I will not stand for such rudeness'. (3) To be a candidate for office — 'stand for Parliament'. (4) To support a principle — 'she stands for honesty in public life'.
note: A genuinely multi-sense phrasal verb; the exam-worthy trap is sense (2), the tolerate sense.

meaning: To make even the slightest effort or exertion. Used almost exclusively in the negative — 'he would not stir a finger to help us' means he did absolutely nothing.
note: Variant of the commoner 'lift a finger' / 'raise a finger'. Same meaning, same negative-only use.

idiom: Struck a chill to the heart
meaning: To cause a sudden stab of fear or dread — to fill someone with foreboding, so that the news or sight seems to freeze them.
note: Dictionary form is 'strike a chill to someone's heart' (or 'strike terror into'); the heading is in the past tense.

meaning: To go through repeated spells of difficulty or bad luck — periods when things go wrong or performance falls off.
note: The fixed idiom is 'hit / go through a bad patch' (singular). 'Struck' and the plural are the deck's own inflection; the sense is unchanged but the headword is non-standard.

meaning: To believe exactly what someone says and act on it at once, without asking for proof or allowing that they may have spoken loosely — so that they are held to the offer or promise they made.
note: ARCHAIC PRONOUNS. The living form is 'take someone at their word'. The 'thee/thy' form is Shakespearean and probably lifted from a text rather than chosen as a headword.

meaning: To occupy space — commonly with the implication that the thing occupies room to no purpose, being useless clutter ('those old files just take up space'). Of a person, it can mean to be a mere encumbrance.
note: The slash in the heading is the deck offering two interchangeable nouns, not a corruption. A newer, positive sense also exists — 'take up space' meaning to assert one's right to be present and be heard — which is the opposite valence and could confuse a learner.

meaning: To discuss a matter thoroughly with someone before deciding — 'we talked it over and agreed'. Also (b) to win someone round by argument, and (c) to speak across someone so that they cannot be heard.
note: Sense (a) is the primary one. Note the syntax differs by sense: you talk a MATTER over, but you talk a PERSON over/round, and you talk over a person who is speaking.
